text: The assembly will hear an address by his
excellency Mihal Martin Tishuk of
Ireland. I request protocol to escort
his excellency and invite him to address
the assembly.
President of the General Assembly.
Distinguished Heads of State and
Government, Secretary General,
Excellency Accord, Friends, the United
Nations is entering its ninth decade at
a moment of great uncertainty and
challenge for the global community.
Conflicts are having devastating effects
on the most vulnerable. The impacts of
the climate crisis are felt in every
corner of our world. Hard one rights are
being rolled back. narrow self-interest
is breaking the bonds of solidarity
which have so often lifted us to
meaningful progress. The international
legal order is under tremendous strain.
New and emerging technologies that offer
unlimited potential could also without
human intervention create unprecedented
dangers. In such moments of uncertainty,
it can be easy to question our
foundations, to retreat, to turn inward,
to say that international cooperation is
too difficult, that multilateralism does
not work, that the problems of others
are not our problems. But that would be
the wrong conclusion because the answer
to a world under strain is not less
international cooperation. It is more.
The answer to the weakening of
principles is not to abandon them. It is
to defend them. And if our multilateral
system is not working effectively, the
answer is not to walk away from it. It
is to make it stronger, fairer, and fit
for the world we live in. That is
Ireland's position and that is what all
of us as members of the United Nations
need to deliver on. We should also
remember what our collective commitment
to the United Nations has achieved.
The multilateral system anchored in the
United Nations charter has been the
foundation of many of humanity's
greatest achievements. It has driven
advances in poverty alleviation, health
care, education, social protection, and
food and nutrition security. It has
championed human rights and dignity and
insisted that accountability matters. It
has given voice to the marginalized.
Mr. President, the people of Ireland
understand that we live in an
interdependent world, that the
challenges we face are interconnected,
cross borders, and require collective
solutions.
Ireland currently holds the presidency
of the Council of the European Union.
Our stewardship of the European Union's
agenda is deeply rooted in the principle
of strength with unity. And this
principle is at the heart of our vision
for the United Nations.
as well as our unwavering commitment to
the pillars which guide its work, peace
and security, human rights and
development. These pillars equally bear
the weight of our shared ambition for a
better, fairer and peaceful world.
Collectively, however, we are not
delivering on their ambition. We are not
staying the course. At a time when
global needs are increasing and becoming
more complex, our responsibility to act
does not diminish. Mr. President, the
denial of the fundamental human rights
of millions of people around the world
remains one of the defining challenges
of our time. Renewed pressure on women's
rights and gender equality is putting
hard one progress at risk. Women and
girls are being told that their
ambitions, their education, their
voices, and their very presence in
public life are unacceptable.
The situation in Afghanistan is one of
the clearest examples of this. The
systematic exclusion of women and girls
from education, employment, and public
life is not something that the
international community can simply
observe from a distance. It is a
profound human rights crisis. Girls are
being denied the education that should
shape their futures. Women are being
denied the ability to work, to
participate fully in society and to
contribute to the economic and social
life of their country. Their freedoms
are being progressively erased and the
world must not become inured to it. We
must not allow the absence of headlines
to become an absence of action. The
women of Afghanistan have not
disappeared and neither should our
solidarity. The same is true elsewhere.
Across the world, women and girls face
conflict related sexual violence, force
displacement, trafficking, and
discrimination. Across the world, LGBTQI
plus people face growing threats to
their rights, safety, and dignity.
Ireland remains firmly committed to the
universality, indivisibility, and equal
application of human rights. These
principles are beyond question. That
commitment is why Ireland is seeking
election to the human rights council for
the 2027 2029 term. And if elected, we
will use that seat to defend the
principle that human rights belong to
everyone everywhere.
Mr. President, today's Russia's legal
today today Russia's legal war in
Ukraine is more deadly for civilians
than at any point since the start of
their full-scale invasion. Russia's
reckless drone and missile attacks on
Ukrainian towns and cities continue to
intensify. These are not the actions of
a country interested in peace. Russia
could halt its brutal attacks at any
time. Yet, it refuses to do so. Russia's
actions have already had direct global
impact in increased food and energy
costs. This time last year, a bushel of
wheat was just over $5. This year, it's
more than $7. The fact that a permanent
member of the security council is
seeking to change bo borders by force in
clear violation of the UN charter is
utterly unacceptable.
Sovereignty and territorial integrity
apply equally to all states. The
international community must remain
steadfast in our response in support of
the UN charter and of a comprehensive,
just and lasting peace. Ireland stands
in solidarity with Ukraine and will
continue to do so. We will continue to
support efforts to hold Russia
accountable for its actions. There can
be no impunity for war crimes. Not in
Ukraine, not anywhere. And that is why
Ireland is a steadfast supporter of the
International Criminal Court. Ireland
strongly opposes efforts to undermine
the court. All measures against it
should be immediately withdrawn.
The international legal order founded on
our agreements to make the world a safer
and more secure place is being
challenged. International law represents
the collective lessons drawn from
conflict, suffering, and atrocity. The
rules and institutions that we have
built over generations exist to protect
the rights, security, and sovereignty of
all states and all peoples. When these
principles are disregarded, the
consequences extend far beyond any
single conflict. We all become less
secure.
Mr. President, 20 years ago, the
Commission on War crimes and crimes
against humanity in Darur saw the
international community come together to
fulfill our collective responsibility to
protect. Despite the extraordinary
efforts of the Sudin people, the cycle
of violence has continued. The conflict
has been inflamed and prolonged by
harmful outside interference.
All states and external actors must
cease arming, financing, and enabling
the war in Sudan.
15 million Sudi Sudin people are
displaced from their homes. Over 19 and
a half million face crisis levels of
hunger. 33 million need urgent
humanitarian assistance.
Violations of international law,
including targeting on the basis of
ethnicity, deliberate destruction of the
means of survival, killing, torture, and
sexual violence are again being used as
weapons of war. We need to act
decisively to support the people of
Sudan to end this conflict. We must
support their aspirations for democracy,
justice, and development. Sudan has
become a forgotten war despite its
devastating impacts. We must not allow
the absence of daily headlines to become
a license for inaction. The people of
Sudan deserve the same attention,
urgency, and solidarity that we rightly
extend to crises elsewhere.
Mr. President, despite its prevalence,
we cannot ever allow ourselves to become
indifferent to conflict and the human
suffering it brings. To do so would deny
the shared humanity of its victims. The
peace plan on Gaza agreed last October
was welcome, but it has not
fundamentally changed the reality on the
ground.
Israeli strikes continue. Humanitarian
aid remains blocked. Civilians continue
to suffer. We, the collected
international community, have failed
Palestine. Ireland, like most gathered
here, believe that the only viable
solution to the decades of conflict,
misery, and wasted human lives, is a
situation where a state of Palestine and
a state of Israel live side by side in
peace, security, and dignity. There are
modest signs of progress. More countries
have recognized the state of Palestine.
An overwhelming majority of UN member
states has endorsed the New York
declaration.
More of us have taken steps to push back
against the illegal and violent settler
occupation of Palestinian land in the
West Bank. But time is running out. What
we are witnessing on the ground is a
deliberate attempt by some to make the
prospect of a two-state solution
impossible.
This is not some mad conspiracy theory.
It is the stated intent of the prime
minister of Israel who said clearly that
and I quote, "We are going to fulfill
our promise that there will be no
Palestinian state. This place belongs to
us." As he permitted the E1 illegal
development in East Jerusalem, and the
situation in Gaza remains an affront to
all that is decent. How can we tolerate
a situation where civilians are so
desperate for shelter that that they
have to make their homes in war damaged
and unsafe buildings? Where eight
children died because one of them
collapsed. Where the most basic
humanitarian aid, food and shelter is
deliberately impeded.
When the full truth of what has
happened, what is still happening in
Gaza is finally known. When the evidence
is gathered, when the testimonies are
heard, when the true horrors are finally
and fully revealed, it will shame the
world. Nobody will be able to say that
we did not know. Let it not be said that
we did not act.
in the West Bank.
In the West Bank, the relentless
expansion of settlements have reached
the scale without precedent, further
eroding, eroding the prospects for a
just and lasting peace. Violent settlers
continue to act with near total impunity
while Palestinian communities face a
sustained campaign of displacement and
destruction amounting to ethnic
cleansing. Entire villages have been
raised, homes and vital infrastructure
demolished and thousands of Palestinian
families driven from the places they
have called home for generations and
exposed to intimidation and violence.
The United Nations reports that this
year there have been almost 200 attacks
against Palestinians every month. A
stark reminder of a reality that is
deepening conflict, suffering, and
despair. The International Court of
Justice has been clear. Settlements in
occupied Palestinian territory are
illegal. Ireland has acted alongside
others to prohibit the import of
settlement goods. It is never too late
to uphold international law.
Mr. President, the conflict in the Gulf
remains deeply concerning and is having
a serious impact around the world. We
need to get back to meaningful goodfaith
negotiations by all sides. Ireland has
consistently stated that Iran must cease
its attacks on its neighbors and also
end its destabilizing activities across
the region, including strikes on ships
in the Strait of Hermuz. Vessels must be
allowed to transit the strait safely and
without tolls in line with international
law. If we are to build greater
stability, Iran must never have a
nuclear weapon. Iran's destabilizing
influence across the region must cease.
We need dialogue to achieve a negotiated
settlement. Mr. President, since 1978,
Irish soldiers have served with
distinction in Lebanon in the unif
peacekeeping operation. Ireland will
continue to work with Lebanon, European
Union, and international partners to
support Lebanon's future peace and
security.
We have consistently condemned
Hezbollah's attacks on Israel, which
must cease immediately. Israel must
withdraw its military presence from
southern Lebanon and bring an end to its
military operations there. Israel's
response has been wholly
disproportionate.
We honor the courage, professionalism,
and dedication of all peacekeepers who
have served under the United Nations. We
remember with particular respect those
who lost their lives in the cause of
peace. We welcome the Secretary
General's report on the future of
peacekeeping and Ireland will work with
others to ensure that this essential
capacity adapts to the 21st century.
Ireland also welcomes wider reforms in
efforts in the United Nations system.
These are necessary if we are to meet
the challenges of our rapidly changing
world. But it is it is also necessary to
point out that no reform process can
succeed unless member states are
prepared to support the United Nations
politically, financially and through
their actions. We need the security
council to live up to its mandate and
respond to the crisis around us. Too
long, the veto has stmmied the council
and eroded its legitimacy. The council's
membership must also finally be made
representative of the world we live in,
starting with the historic
underrepresentation of African countries
and ensuring that the voices of small
and the most vulnerable states are
heard. Mr. President, I conclude by
thanking Secretary General Antonio
Gutierrez for his principal leadership
and steadfast commitment to the United
Nations over the past decade. I
especially commend his courage in
tackling the climate crisis, the
fundamental issue of our time. From
devastating floods in Nepal to wildfires
across Europe, communities are
increasingly experiencing the
consequences of a ch a changing climate.
The Paris Agreement remains a powerful
example of what can be achieved when
countries work together. Secretary
Gutierz has been a vital voice in
calling member states to action. We look
forward to working with the next
Secretary General in advancing the
charter's principles and strengthening
this institution.
As the leader of a country that fought
for its independence and its place among
nations, I'm deeply conscious conscious
of the inheritance we have received. The
United Nations, for all its
imperfections, remains one of humanity's
greatest achievements, a testament to
the belief that peace, dignity, and
progress are best secured when nations
work together. At a time when that
belief is under strain, it is our shared
responsibility to renew it, strengthen
it, and ensure it endures for
generations to come. Thank you very much
indeed.
On behalf of the assembly, I wish to
thank the teach of Ireland.
